decks.title: Cell Biology
decks.subject: Biology
decks.description: Cell structure, microscopy, transport and cell division.

cards.front: What is the function of the nucleus?
cards.back: Contains DNA/genetic material and controls the activities of the cell.

cards.front: What is the function of mitochondria?
cards.back: Site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy for the cell.

cards.front: What is the function of ribosomes?
What does the cell membrane do?
cards.back: Controls which substances enter and leave the cell.

cards.front: Which organelles are found in plant cells but NOT animal cells?
cards.back: Cell wall, permanent vacuole and chloroplasts.

cards.front: What is the cell wall of a plant made from?
What is the function of chloroplasts?
cards.back: Contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis.
Jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions in the cell happen.

cards.front: How do prokaryotic cells differ from eukaryotic cells?
cards.back: Prokaryotes have no nucleus; their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm.

cards.front: Give an example of a prokaryote.

cards.back: Net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
Diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.
Movement of substances from a low to a high concentration against the gradient, using energy from respiration.
An undifferentiated cell that can divide and differentiate into specialised cell types.
The process by which a cell becomes specialised for its job.
A cell divides to produce two genetically identical diploid daughter cells (used for growth and repair).
A series of stages: DNA replication, mitosis, then cytokinesis (cell splits in two).

cards.front: Which type of microscope has higher magnification and resolution: light or electron?

cards.back: Cell division producing four genetically different haploid gametes.

cards.front: Name two adaptations of a root hair cell.
cards.back: Long thin extension giving a large surface area; many mitochondria for active transport.

decks.title: Genetics & Evolution
decks.subject: Biology
decks.description: DNA, inheritance, variation and natural selection.

cards.front: What are the four bases in DNA?
Which bases pair together in DNA?
cards.back: A with T; C with G.
A short section of DNA that codes for a particular protein.
The entire genetic material of an organism.
A different version of the same gene.
The allele that is expressed even if only one copy is present.
Having two identical alleles for a gene.
Having two different alleles for a gene.
The combination of alleles an organism has.
The observable characteristics that result from the genotype and environment.

cards.front: Cross Bb × Bb: what ratio of dominant to recessive phenotype?
How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
How many chromosomes are in a human gamete?
Which chromosomes determine sex in humans?
Name a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele.

cards.back: Individuals with beneficial characteristics are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on those alleles.

cards.front: Who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?

cards.back: A random change in the DNA base sequence of a gene.
Humans choose parents with desired characteristics to breed together over many generations.
Transferring a gene from one organism into another so it has the desired characteristic.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

decks.title: Human Body Systems
decks.subject: Biology
decks.description: Digestion, circulation, breathing, nervous system and hormones.

cards.front: Which enzyme breaks down starch, and where is it made?
cards.back: Amylase, made in the salivary glands and pancreas.
Lipase, producing fatty acids and glycerol.
Emulsifies fat to increase its surface area and neutralises stomach acid.

cards.front: Where is bile made and stored?
cards.back: Made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder.

cards.front: Where does most absorption of food happen?
cards.back: The small intestine (villi give a large surface area).

cards.front: What are the four chambers of the heart?
cards.back: Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.

cards.front: Which blood vessel carries blood from the heart to the lungs?
Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
cards.back: It pumps blood around the whole body at higher pressure.
Carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.

cards.front: Name the three types of blood vessel.
What do red blood cells do?
cards.back: Carry oxygen using haemoglobin; they have no nucleus and a biconcave shape.

cards.front: What do white blood cells do?
cards.back: Defend against pathogens by phagocytosis and by producing antibodies and antitoxins.

cards.front: What is the site of gas exchange in the lungs?
What is the path of a nerve impulse in a reflex arc?
cards.back: Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector.
Maintaining a constant internal environment (temperature, water, glucose).

decks.title: Photosynthesis & Respiration
decks.subject: Biology
decks.description: How plants make food and how all organisms release energy.

cards.back: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in light, using chlorophyll).
Endothermic – it takes in energy from light.

cards.front: Name three limiting factors of photosynthesis.
cards.back: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature.

cards.front: How do plants use the glucose they make?

cards.back: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy).

cards.front: Word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscles?
cards.back: Glucose → lactic acid (+ small amount of energy).

cards.front: Word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast?

cards.back: Extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the lactic acid.

cards.front: Which is more efficient: aerobic or anaerobic respiration?
cards.back: Aerobic respiration releases much more energy per glucose.
Pores in the leaf that let gases in and out; opened and closed by guard cells.
Water and minerals from the roots up to the leaves.
Dissolved sugars (sucrose) around the plant – translocation.
Evaporation of water from leaves, drawing more water up through the plant.

cards.front: What test shows the presence of starch?
cards.back: Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black.
To make amino acids and proteins.

decks.title: Atomic Structure & Periodic Table
decks.subject: Chemistry
decks.description: Protons, neutrons, electrons, isotopes and the periodic table.

cards.front: What is the relative charge and mass of a proton?
What is the relative charge and mass of a neutron?
What is the relative charge and mass of an electron?
Where are protons and neutrons found?

cards.back: The number of protons in an atom (also the number of electrons in a neutral atom).
The total number of protons plus neutrons.

cards.front: How do you work out the number of neutrons?

cards.back: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

cards.front: What is the electron configuration of sodium (Z = 11)?
What is the electron configuration of chlorine (Z = 17)?
How many electrons fit in the first three shells?
Who first proposed the 'plum pudding' model?
What did Rutherford's gold foil experiment show?
cards.back: Most of an atom is empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.

cards.front: Who suggested electrons orbit in shells?
How are elements arranged in the modern periodic table?
cards.back: In order of increasing atomic number, with similar properties in the same group.

cards.front: What do elements in the same group have in common?
cards.back: The same number of outer-shell electrons, so similar chemical properties.

cards.front: How does reactivity change down Group 1?
cards.back: It increases – the outer electron is lost more easily.

cards.front: How does reactivity change down Group 7?
cards.back: It decreases – it's harder to gain an electron.

cards.front: What are Group 0 elements and why are they unreactive?
cards.back: The noble gases – they have full outer shells.

decks.title: Bonding & Structure
decks.subject: Chemistry
decks.description: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, plus giant structures.

cards.back: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by transfer of electrons.
A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
Attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.

cards.front: Which types of elements form ionic compounds?
Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
cards.back: Strong electrostatic forces between ions need lots of energy to overcome.

cards.front: When can ionic compounds conduct electricity?
cards.back: When molten or dissolved – the ions are free to move.

cards.front: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting points?
cards.back: Weak intermolecular forces are broken, not the strong covalent bonds.

cards.front: Why can't simple molecules conduct electricity?
cards.back: They have no overall charge and no free charged particles.
Each carbon is bonded to four others in a rigid giant covalent lattice – very hard.
Each carbon bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom.
A single layer of graphite, one atom thick.
A hollow-shaped carbon molecule, e.g. buckminsterfullerene C₆₀.
Layers of ions can slide over each other.

cards.front: Why do metals conduct electricity and heat?
cards.back: Delocalised electrons carry charge and energy.
A mixture of a metal with another element; harder than pure metals as layers can't slide easily.

cards.front: What charge does a Group 1 ion have?
What charge does a Group 2 ion have?
What charge does a Group 7 ion have?
What is the formula of magnesium oxide?
What is the formula of calcium chloride?
How many covalent bonds does carbon usually form?

cards.back: A particle 1–100 nm in size, with a very high surface-area-to-volume ratio.

decks.title: Acids, Bases & Reactions
decks.subject: Chemistry
decks.description: pH, neutralisation, salts, rates and energy changes.

cards.front: What ion do acids produce in water?
What ion do alkalis produce in water?
Which pH values are acidic, neutral and alkaline?
What salt does hydrochloric acid make?
What salt does sulfuric acid make?
What salt does nitric acid make?
What is neutralisation in ionic terms?
What is the test for hydrogen gas?
cards.back: A lit splint makes a squeaky pop.

cards.front: What is the test for carbon dioxide?
cards.back: Bubble through limewater – it turns cloudy.

cards.front: What is the test for oxygen?
What is the test for chlorine?
cards.back: Damp blue litmus paper is bleached white.
Releases energy to the surroundings; temperature rises.
Takes in energy from the surroundings; temperature falls.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.

cards.front: Name four factors that affect rate of reaction.
cards.back: Temperature, concentration/pressure, surface area, and catalysts.

cards.front: What does a reversible reaction look like in an equation?
What is oxidation in terms of electrons?
cards.back: Loss of electrons (OILRIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).

cards.front: What happens at the cathode during electrolysis?
What is the law of conservation of mass?
cards.back: No atoms are made or lost in a reaction, so total mass of reactants = total mass of products.

decks.title: Computer Science Fundamentals
decks.subject: Computer Science
decks.description: Hardware, binary, networks, security and algorithms.

cards.front: What does CPU stand for and what does it do?
cards.back: Central Processing Unit – fetches, decodes and executes instructions.

cards.front: What are the three stages of the fetch–decode–execute cycle?
cards.back: Fetch an instruction from memory, decode it, then execute it.
Volatile main memory that temporarily stores data and programs currently in use.
Non-volatile memory that stores the boot-up instructions (BIOS).

cards.front: What is the difference between volatile and non-volatile memory?
cards.back: Volatile memory loses its contents when power is off; non-volatile keeps them.
The Arithmetic Logic Unit – performs calculations and logical comparisons.
Very fast memory inside or near the CPU that stores frequently used data.

cards.front: How many bits are in a byte?
How many bytes are in a kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte?
cards.back: 1 KB = 1000 B, 1 MB = 1000 KB, 1 GB = 1000 MB (decimal, as in GCSE).
A compact way to represent binary (e.g. colour codes, memory addresses).
A character set that represents text characters using 7-bit binary codes.
The smallest individual point of an image.
Reduces file size by permanently removing some data (e.g. JPEG, MP3).

cards.front: What is a LAN vs a WAN?
cards.back: LAN covers a small area (e.g. a school); WAN covers a large geographical area (e.g. the Internet).

cards.front: What does an IP address identify?

cards.back: Fraudulent emails or messages that trick people into revealing sensitive data.
Software or hardware that monitors and blocks unauthorised network traffic.
A step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem.

cards.front: How does a binary search work?
cards.back: Repeatedly halves a sorted list by checking the middle item.

cards.front: How does a bubble sort work?
cards.back: Repeatedly compares adjacent items and swaps them if out of order.

cards.front: What are the three basic programming constructs?
What is the difference between a compiler and an interpreter?
cards.back: A compiler translates all the code at once; an interpreter translates and runs it line by line.

A browser API for storing key/value strings that persist across sessions.

cards.back: A word that names a person, place, thing or idea.
A word that describes an action, event or state.
A word that describes a noun.

A word that replaces a noun: he, she, it, they.

A word showing relationship in place or time: on, under, before.
A group of words containing a subject and a verb.
A clause that makes sense on its own.
A clause that depends on a main clause to make sense.

cards.front: When do you use a semicolon?
cards.back: To join two closely related main clauses, or to separate items in a complex list.

cards.front: When do you use a colon?
cards.back: To introduce a list, explanation or quotation after a complete clause.

cards.front: What is the difference between 'its' and 'it's'?
What is the difference between 'their', 'there' and 'they're'?
cards.back: Their = belonging to them; there = place; they're = they are.

cards.front: What is the difference between 'your' and 'you're'?
cards.back: Your = belonging to you; you're = you are.

cards.front: Where does the apostrophe go in 'the dogs' bones' (several dogs)?

cards.back: Fewer for countable items; less for uncountable amounts.
When the subject receives the action: 'The ball was kicked by Sam.'
When the subject performs the action: 'Sam kicked the ball.'
Incorrectly joining two main clauses with just a comma.

cards.front: What is the difference between 'affect' and 'effect'?
cards.back: Affect is usually a verb (to influence); effect is usually a noun (a result).
A word or phrase at the start of a sentence describing the action, followed by a comma.

decks.subject: English
decks.description: Name the technique – and explain its effect.

cards.back: Repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words: 'peter piper picked'.
Repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words: 'the rain in Spain'.
A word that imitates the sound it describes: 'crash', 'buzz'.
Compares two things using 'like' or 'as': 'brave as a lion'.
States that one thing IS another: 'the world is a stage'.
Giving human qualities to a non-human thing: 'the wind whispered'.
Deliberate exaggeration for effect: 'I've told you a million times'.
Weather or nature reflecting the mood: 'storm clouds gathered as he grieved'.
Placing two contrasting things side by side to highlight differences.
Hints at events that will happen later in the story.
A contrast between expectation and reality.
When the audience knows something the characters do not.
Language that creates a picture or sensory experience in the reader's mind.
Using an object, colour or image to represent a bigger idea.
A recurring image, idea or symbol that develops a theme.
An indirect reference to another text, person, or event.
A mild expression used in place of something harsh: 'passed away'.
A question asked for effect, not expecting an answer.
Repeating a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses.
A list of three words or phrases for emphasis and rhythm.
A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud, alone on stage.
A sentence running over a line break in poetry without punctuation.
A pause in the middle of a line of poetry, often shown by punctuation.

decks.title: Rivers, Coasts & Tectonics
decks.subject: Geography
decks.description: Physical geography – landforms and processes.

cards.front: What is the source of a river?
cards.back: Where it begins, usually in upland areas.
Where the river meets the sea.
A smaller river that joins a larger one.
The point where two rivers meet.
The boundary of high land separating one drainage basin from another.

cards.front: Name the four processes of river erosion.
What is a waterfall formed by?
cards.back: A band of hard rock overlying softer rock that erodes faster, forming a plunge pool.
Erosion on the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank of a bend.
A meander cut off when the river breaks through the neck of a bend.
Flat land beside a river that floods when the river overflows.
Zigzag movement of sediment along a coast by waves hitting at an angle.

cards.front: How is a wave-cut platform formed?
cards.back: A cliff is undercut and collapses, leaving a flat rocky platform.
Hard rock is left sticking out as softer rock erodes into bays.
A narrow ridge of sand or shingle joined to land at one end, formed by deposition.

cards.front: What are the layers of the Earth?
cards.back: Inner core, outer core, mantle and crust.

cards.front: What is a constructive plate margin?
cards.back: Two plates move apart; magma rises to form new crust.

cards.front: What is a destructive plate margin?
cards.back: An oceanic plate subducts beneath a continental plate, forming volcanoes and trenches.

cards.front: What is a conservative plate margin?
cards.back: Plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes (e.g. San Andreas Fault).

cards.front: What is the focus of an earthquake?
cards.back: The point underground where the earthquake starts; the epicentre is directly above.

cards.front: What is the Ring of Fire?
cards.back: A belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean.

cards.front: How long does light from the Sun take to reach Earth?

decks.title: How to Learn (Study Skills)

decks.description: The science of effective revision – use these on this very app!

cards.back: Testing yourself from memory instead of re-reading – flashcards are perfect for this.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals just as you're about to forget it.

Mixing different topics or problem types in one study session.

Explain a concept in simple words as if teaching a beginner to find gaps in your understanding.

cards.front: Why is sleep important for revision?
cards.back: Sleep helps consolidate memories, so revising before bed and sleeping well improves recall.
A diagram that links ideas around a central topic using branches and keywords.
Combining words with visuals (diagrams, drawings) to aid memory.
A memory aid such as an acronym or rhyme (e.g. 'Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain').

cards.front: Why is cramming less effective than spacing out revision?
cards.back: Crammed knowledge fades quickly; spaced sessions build longer-lasting memory.

cards.front: What should you do with cards you rate 'Again' in this app?
cards.back: Review them soon – they come back in the next session until you know them.

Which countries made up the Triple Alliance?
